of the wetland where trench plugs are not practical. To prevent affecting hydrology of wetlands
that may be subject to drainage as a result of water following the pipeline along the trench and
having a French drain effect, permanent trench breakers will be installed at the boundaries of
wetlands to maintain wetland hydrology.
In unfarmed wetlands that are not saturated at the time of construction, WBI Energy will segregate
topsoil from the trench line to protect its integrity and help preserve the seed bank. Segregating
the topsoil should preserve the potential for natural revegetation of the right-of-way to its
preconstruction plant community. Trench spoil excavated in wetlands, in most cases, will be
stored in the construction corridor adjacent to where it was excavated. In areas where excavated
trench spoil may flow into undisturbed areas of the wetland, silt fence, straw bales, or other
appropriate sedimentation control devices will be installed at the edges of the construction right-
of-way to prevent sediment migration.
Following pipeline installation, the trench will be backfilled with material excavated within the
wetland and preconstruction contours will be restored to the maximum extent practicable.
Additionally, WBI Energy will replace segregated topsoil to the surface layer of the trench during
backfilling. Replacing the wetland topsoil and restoring preconstruction hydrology will promote
re-establishment of wetland vegetation. Following construction, WBI Energy will monitor
restoration of unfarmed wetland plant communities, in accordance with the FERC Procedures.
In saturated wetlands where soils are unable to support equipment and safely excavate the
trench, temporary work surfaces of timber mats or travel pads will be installed adjacent to the
pipeline trench. Construction will proceed as in unsaturated wetlands, except topsoil will not be
segregated due to the saturated conditions where these conditions are present. Pipe stringing
and fabrication may occur within the wetland adjacent to the trench, or in a designated extra
workspace adjacent to the wetland.
In accordance with the FERC Procedures, WBI Energy will construct the pipeline facilities across
farmed wetlands using the same methods as adjacent farmed uplands. Most seasonally
saturated farmed wetlands are used for crop production and, in these areas, topsoil will be
segregated in the same manner as topsoil in upland agricultural lands. Pipe stringing and
fabrication will generally occur within the farmed wetland adjacent to the trench, or adjacent to
the farmed wetland in a designated ATWS.
Inadvertent spills of chemicals used during construction, such as fuels, lubricants, and solvents,
may contaminate wetland soils and vegetation if inadvertently spilled during construction in
wetlands. To minimize the potential for spills in wetlands, and any impacts from such spills, WBI
Energy will implement the measures identified in its SPCC Plan (see appendix 1F of Resource
Report 1).
During construction, erosion and sediment controls will be placed where necessary along the
pipeline rights-of-way and surrounding extra workspaces to minimize impacts on adjacent
unfarmed wetlands in accordance with the FERC Plan, FERC Procedures, and applicable
permits. Erosion and sedimentation barriers will be installed and maintained throughout the
construction period to prevent disturbed soils and sediment from migrating into adjacent
undisturbed wetland areas. During trench-dewatering activities, water will be filtered to remove
sediments and dewatering will occur outside of wetlands within well vegetated upland areas.

2.4    CUMULATIVE IMPACTS
Cumulative impacts represent the incremental accumulation of past, present, and reasonably
foreseeable future actions on the environment (40 CFR 1508.7). Cumulative impacts may result
when a single action continuously impacts the environment, multiple actions impact the same
resource over a period of time, or direct impacts on one resource result in indirect impacts on a
different resource. Although the individual impacts of each separate action might not be
significant, the additive or synergistic impacts of multiple actions could be significant. An analysis
of the potential cumulative impacts of the Project will be provided with WBI Energy’s FERC
application.

                               WBI ENERGY TRANSMISSION, INC.
                              BAKKEN EAST PIPELINE PROJECT
                     RESOURCE REPORT 3 – FISH, WILDLIFE, AND VEGETATION

Minimum Filing Requirements:                                                                             Addressed In:

1.Classify the fishery type of each surface waterbody that would be crossed, including fisheries         Section 3.4 and Resource
of special concern - Title 18 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part (§) 380.12(e)(1)             Report 2 section 2.2.2

2.Describe terrestrial and wetland wildlife and habitats that would be affected by the project - 18      Sections 3.2.1.1 and 3.4.1.1
CFR § 380.12(e)(2)

3.Describe the major vegetative cover types that would be crossed and provide the acreage of             Sections 3.1.1 and table 3.1.1-1
each vegetative cover type that would be affected by construction - 18 CFR § 380.12(e)(3)

4. Describe the effects of construction and operation procedures on the fishery resources and            Section 3.4.2
proposed mitigation measures - 18 CFR § 380.12(e)(4)

5. Evaluate the potential for short-term, long-term, and permanent impact on the wildlife                Sections 3.2 and 3.5
resources and state-listed endangered or threatened species caused by construction and
operation of the project and proposed mitigation measures - 18 CFR § 380.12(e)(4)

6. Identify all federally listed or proposed endangered or threatened species that potentially           Sections 3.5.1 and appendix 3D
occur in the vicinity of the project and discuss the results of the consultations with other
agencies. Include survey reports as specified in 18 CFR § 380.12(e)(5)

7. Identify all federally listed essential fish habitat that potentially occurs in the vicinity of the   Not applicable
project and the results of abbreviated consultations with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric
Administration’s National Marine Fisheries Service, and any resulting essential fish habitat
assessment - 18 CFR § 380.12(e)(6)

8. Describe any significant biological resources that would be affected. Describe impact and             Sections 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, and 3.5
any mitigation proposed to avoid or minimize that impact - 18 CFR § 380.12(e)(4,7)


Additional Information:                                                                                  Addressed In:

Provide a list of significant wildlife habitats crossed by the project. Specify locations by             Section 3.2.1
milepost, and include length and width of crossing at each significant wildlife habitat

Provide a description of project-specific measures that would be implemented during                      Section 3.3.2
construction and operation of the project to avoid or minimize impacts on migratory birds.
Include comments from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service on the proposed measures.

For aquatic and marine species, be sure to include effects of sedimentation, changes to                  Section 3.4.2
substrate, effects of blasting, etc. This information may be needed on a location-specific (i.e.,
milepost) basis and may require geophysical and other surveys. Results of such surveys and
analyses should be included in the application.

3.0       RESOURCE REPORT 3: FISH, WILDLIFE, AND VEGETATION
In accordance with Title 18 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 380.12(e), Resource
Report 3 provides information regarding fisheries, wildlife, and vegetation that may be in the
vicinity of WBI Energy Transmission, Inc.’s proposed Bakken East Pipeline Project (Project). This
information was developed through literature reviews, consultation with agency personnel, and
field surveys. Resource Report 3 describes how the Project may affect these resources and
outlines proposed measures to avoid, minimize, or mitigate impacts.

3.1       VEGETATION RESOURCES
This section describes the existing vegetation cover types that occur within the Project area,
including natural vegetation communities, common plant species in each community, cultivated
or managed vegetation, and exotic or invasive species. Potential impacts on vegetation
resources from construction and operation of the Project are also described. Special status plant
species, including federally listed species, are discussed in section 3.5. Wetland communities
identified along the pipeline routes are identified in table 2.3.1-1 and described in section 2.3 of
Resource Report 2. Information on vegetation types within the Project area was obtained from
available literature, results of environmental field surveys, and review of recent (2020) digital
aerial photography.
3.1.1     Existing Vegetation

The proposed pipeline extends from west to east across nearly the entire state of North Dakota,
crossing the following counties: McKenzie, Dunn, Mercer, Oliver, Burleigh, Kidder, Stutsman,
Barnes, and Cass Counties. It also crosses all five of the major ecoregions of North Dakota
identified in the North Dakota Game and Fish Department (NDGFD) State Wildlife Action Plan
(SWAP), as modified from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Level IV Ecoregions
(NDGFD, 2025a; EPA, 2025). From west to east, they include the Badlands, Missouri Slope,
Missouri Coteau, Drift Prairie, and Red River Valley Ecoregions (NDGFD, 2025a; 2025b). These
ecoregions are further detailed below:

      •   Badlands – The Badlands consist of a rugged landscape of buttes, rock outcrops,
          washouts, and hardwood draws along the banks of the Little Missouri River. The region
          is defined by poor soils, steep slopes, high erosion, and shortgrass prairie.

      •   Missouri Slope – The Missouri Slope’s sandstone and shale layers were mostly untouched
          by the glaciers that shaped eastern North Dakota. The area features an irregular
          topography, with occasional buttes rising above the landscape and complex drainage
          systems. Livestock ranching dominates the region, although small grain, corn and
          sunflower farming is also practiced.

      •   Missouri Coteau – The Missouri Coteau extends eastward from the Missouri River to the
          western boundary of the Drift Prairie, marking the western edge of North Dakota’s
          glaciated terrain. Wetlands are abundant along the eastern edge of the Coteau but
          become fewer towards the Missouri River. The predominant land use in this region is a
          mix of small grain, corn, soybean, and sunflower farming, along with livestock ranching.

      •   Drift Prairie – The Drift Prairie stretches diagonally from northwestern to southeastern
          North Dakota. This glaciated landscape appears mostly flat with gentle, washboard-like
          undulations. The soil and climate create a transition zone between shortgrass and
          tallgrass prairie species. The region is dotted with a high concentration of seasonal and

   •   Red River Valley – The Red River forms North Dakota’s eastern border, with the Red River

North Dakota has a continental climate, with average temperatures ranging between 2 to
17 degrees Fahrenheit (°F) in January and 67 to 73°F in July. Annual precipitation levels increase
moving east across the state, ranging from a low of approximately 11 inches per year in the
Badlands and westernmost portion of the Missouri Slope to a high of approximately 19 inches per
year in the Red River Valley (NDGFD, 2025i). Most of the precipitation falls between April through
October, with June being the wettest month (North Dakota State University, 2026).
3.1.1.1 General Vegetation

Most of the vegetative cover in the Project area consists of cultivated crops followed by
herbaceous plant communities (e.g., grasslands). These dominant vegetation types are
intermixed with smaller amounts of shrubland (shrub/scrub); landscaped vegetation on developed

without vegetation); and palustrine emergent (PEM) wetlands. Vegetation association with scrub-
shrub (PSS) wetlands, forested (PFO) wetlands, open water, and deciduous, evergreen, and
mixed forests each make up less than 1 percent of the Project area.

developed lands consist of introduced turf grasses, ornamental plants, and unvegetated ground,
they are not further discussed in this section. For further discussion of impacts on cultivated
cropland and developed land, see Resource Report 8.

Grassland (Herbaceous)
Much of the grassland and shrubland in the Project area historically provided habitat for bison but
is now used as rangeland for cattle and other livestock. This change has altered the plant
communities in the area due to a different grazing regime than that of bison, overgrazing, and
introduced forage grass species (Towne et al., 2005).
Common non-native grasses in the Project area consist of smooth brome (Bromus inermis) and
Kentucky bluegrass (Poa pratensis) (NDGFD, 2025c). Non-native forbs, like Canada thistle
(Cirsium arvense), are also common throughout the area (NPS, 2024; see section 3.1.1.2). Non-
native grassland appears to have been tilled in the past but is not currently used for agricultural
purposes.
Native prairie is generally divided into three categories including tallgrass, mixed-grass, and
shortgrass communities. Each of these prairie types is dominated by perennial grasses
intermixed with forbs, with shrubs occurring infrequently (NDGFD, 2025c). Tallgrass prairie is
predominantly found in eastern North Dakota in the Red River Valley, although most of the native
tallgrass prairie has been converted to cropland. The Project area will primarily overlap mixed-
grass and shortgrass communities.
Mixed-grass prairie in North Dakota is found within the Missouri Coteau and Drift Prairie
Ecoregions, with transitions to surrounding wetlands. This region is characterized with
hummocky, rolling hills and a high concentration of wetlands including alkaline lakes. Tracts of
native prairie remain, and cattle grazing is extensive on the landscape. Mixed grass prairie
includes a combination of tallgrass and shortgrass species and is dominated by warm and cool
season grasses and sedges. Common grasses include prairie junegrass (Koeleria macrantha),
western wheatgrass (Pascopyrum smithii), green needlegrass (Nassella viridula), needle and
thread (Hesperostipa comata), blue grama (Bouteloua gracilis), little bluestem (Schizachyrium
scoparium), and needleleaf sedge (Carex duriuscula). Mixed-grass prairie includes a variety of
forbs such as pasque flower (Pulsatilla patens), prairie smoke (Geum triflorum), Missouri
milkvetch (Astragalus missouriensis), and purple prairie clover (Dalea purpurea). Shortgrass
prairie is primarily found in the higher elevations within the Missouri Slope Ecoregion. Dominant
species in shortgrass prairie include warm season grasses such as blue grama, needleleaf sedge,
and buffalograss (Bouteloua dactyloides). A variety of forb species are often found in North
Dakota shortgrass prairie and species may include purple locoweed (Oxytropis lambertii), white
wild onion (Allium spp.), prickly pear (Opuntia polyacantha), and white beardtongue (Penstemon
albidus) (NDGFD, 2025c; U.S. Forest Service [USFS] , 2026b).
WBI Energy estimated the extent of native prairie in the Project area based on the North Dakota
Unbroken Grassland database (North Dakota Geographic Information Systems [NDGIS], 2022)
and during the Project Dakota Skipper (DASK) habitat field survey. The NDGFD has differentiated
unbroken grasslands from other grasslands in North Dakota based on available spatial
information of native species diversity and abundance, as well as the absence of indicators of
previous agricultural activities (e.g., tillage patterns in soil and rock piles along margins of fields)
(NDGFD, 2025z). Table 3.1.1-2 provides the acreages of unbroken grasslands identified by the
NDGFD in the Project area by pipeline facility.

Shrubland
Shrubland in North Dakota comprises 681.2 acres (8.5 percent) of the Project area (table 3.1.1-
1). Generally located along terraces of rivers and streams or gentle slopes, shrublands are
dominated by shrub species or mid-height grasses (NatureServe, 2026). Shrubland habitat is
scattered throughout the Missouri Slope, around the Badlands formations (NDGFD, 2025b;
2025d).
Forest
Forests are limited in North Dakota. In 2021, they made up just 2 percent of the land cover in the
state. Forests in North Dakota are primarily deciduous forests dominated by hardwood species
such as green ash (Fraxinus pennsylvanica), bur oak (Quercus macrocarpa), and hickory (Carya
spp.) (USFS, 2021). In the Project area, forests make up approximately 1 percent or 62.2 acres
of the land cover, almost exclusively along riparian corridors except in the badlands at the western
end of the Project (NDGFD, 2025d; table 3.1.1-1). Isolated trees also occur along wetland edges
and in hedgerows along roads or fields. Palustrine forested wetlands are found in the Project
area (see Resource Report 2). In many areas, forests have experienced significant alterations
over the past decades due to the spread of Dutch elm disease, emerald ash borer, overgrazing,
altered water flows, and conversion of the land to other uses (Claeys, 2020). Trees common in
these areas include green ash and eastern cottonwood (Populus deltoides) (Herman, 2003).
Table 3.1.1-1 summarizes the vegetation and other land cover types in the Project area. Land
cover crossed by the Project was classified based U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) National Land
Cover Database (NLCD) data supplemented with data from Project biological field surveys (USGS
2016).
Open Water
Open water comprises 35.9 acres (less than 1 percent) of the Project area (table 3.1.1-1). The
Project will cross 196 waterbodies, the majority of which are intermittent/ephemeral stream
crossings. Stream categorization is further discussed in section 3.4.1. The edges of open water
zones provide habitat for riparian vegetation communities, including shrubs, woodlands, and
wetland or grassland species. Waterbodies crossed by the Project are further detailed in section
2.2.2 of Resource Report 2.

3.1.1.2 Noxious Weeds and Other Invasive Plants

According to regulations in North Dakota law (North Dakota Century Code [NDCC] 4.1-47-01),
noxious weeds are defined as any “plant propagated by either seed or vegetative parts and
determined to be injurious to public health, crops, livestock, land or other property” as determined
by NDCC sections 4.1-47-05, 4.1-47-10, or 4.1-47-21. The North Dakota Department of
Agriculture (NDDA) has established and implemented a statewide network to manage noxious
weeds. Under these regulations (NDCC 4.1-47-02, 4.1-47-28, 4.1-47-30), private landowners are
responsible for the control or cost of control of noxious weeds on their property, and individuals
may not willfully transport any material or equipment on public roads or dispose of material that
contains noxious weeds in a manner that allows for the dissemination of noxious weeds.
Noxious and invasive plant species include non-native, undesirable native, or introduced species
that are able to exclude and/or out-compete desired native vegetation, thereby decreasing overall
species diversity. North Dakota lists 13 statewide noxious weeds that are recognized and
regulated by all cities and counties in North Dakota (NDDA, 2025b). Counties have the option to
add additional weeds onto a list for enforcement in their jurisdictions. Of the counties crossed by
the Project area, only McKenzie, Dunn, and Cass Counties have additional noxious weed species
listed. Table 3.1.1-3 details state and county noxious weeds that are listed for the counties
crossed by the Project.
The NDDA reports estimated acreages of state-listed noxious weed populations documented and
reported by county weed officers. The most commonly occurring noxious weeds in the counties
crossed by the Project include absinth wormwood, Canada thistle, and leafy spurge. The highest
densities of noxious weed acreage were reported in Dunn and Stutsman Counties. Kidder County
had the most noxious weed species reported, with 11 out of the 13 state-listed species
documented (NDDA, 2026).
WBI Energy conducted noxious weed surveys for state- and county-listed noxious weed species
within a 300-foot-wide corridor centered on the proposed pipeline centerlines within grassland
areas. These noxious weed surveys were conducted concurrently with wetland, species, and
other vegetation surveys and were not timed to coincide with any specific morphological state.
Data points and/or polygons were collected at observed noxious weed infestations, and percent
cover was recorded. Weed species identified include Canada thistle (Cirsium arvense (L.) Scop.)
leafy spurge (Euphorbia esula L.), absinth wormwood (Artemisia absinthum L.), and palmer
amaranth (Amaranthus palmeri).

Vegetative aquatic nuisance species (ANS) are regulated under North Dakota Administrative
Code Chapter 30-03-06, which requires that all construction equipment used for in-water work
must be free of prohibited or regulated ANS, as defined in the state's ANS list. Vegetative ANS,
such as curly leaf pondweed (Potamogeton crispus), Eurasian watermilfoil (Myriophyllum
spicatum), and flowering rush (Butomus umbellatus), are tracked and regulated by the NDGFD.
ANS can greatly degrade or ruin habitats and compete with native and/or desirable species for
food and space. Once established, the cost of controlling ANS far exceeds the minimal costs
required to keep from spreading ANS into or within North Dakota. According to the NDGFD
current list of ANS infested waters, the proposed route crosses two waterbodies with confirmed
presence of vegetative ANS species, –the Sheyenne River in Barnes County and the Missouri
River in Oliver County. The Sheyenne River is infested with flowering rush and Eurasian
watermilfoil, and the Missouri River is infested with curly leaf pondweed (NDGFD, 2025e).
3.1.1.3 Conservation Areas

U.S. Department of Agriculture Private Land Easements
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) has two voluntary conservation programs that provide
financial and technical support for the preservation or restoration of native plant communities on
private land: the Conservation Reserve Program (CRP) and the Agricultural Conservation
Easement Program (ACEP). The primary aim of the CRP is to reduce soil erosion and
sedimentation in streams and lakes and establish native grassland, woodland, and riparian habitat
by encouraging conversion of highly erodible cropland or other environmentally sensitive areas

(NRCS, 2026b). The program is administered by the Farm Service Agency, with the Natural
Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) providing technical land eligibility determinations,
conservation planning, and practice implementation.
The ACEP assists landowners, land trusts, and other entities in the protection, restoration, and
enhancement of wetlands by establishing wetland reserve easements on private land (NRCS,
2026a).
As described in more detail in section 8.7 of Resource Report 8, WBI Energy has been consulting
with various agencies and landowners to determine if any CRP lands or ACEP wetland reserve
easements are crossed by the Project. To date, no CRP lands have been identified in the Project
area, and the Project is being rerouted to avoid two ACEP wetland reserve easements. The
results of the ongoing consultation and an assessment of impacts will be included in the final
application. 1
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Conservation Areas
Similar to the USDA, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) provides financial and technical
support to private landowners to establish either grassland easements or wetland easements
(USFWS, 2026d; 2026j). USFWS grassland easements are native grasslands protected from
development and cultivation (USFWS, 2026d), while USFWS wetland easements protects certain
wetlands within the easement tract from draining or other modifications (USFWS, 2026j; see
Resource Report 2 for additional details).
WBI Energy, in coordination with the USFWS, identified a number of both grassland and wetland
easements that will be crossed by a preliminary Project route. WBI Energy was able to adjust the
Project route to avoid grassland easements. While a number of wetland easements are still
crossed within the USFWS Audubon, Long Lake, Chase, and Valley City Wetland Management
Districts, WBI Energy has adjusted the Project route or implemented trenchless construction
techniques (horizontal directional drill [HDD] or bore) to avoid or minimize impacts on the
protected wetland basins within these easements.
In addition, the USFWS acquires properties specifically as Waterfowl Production Areas (WPAs),
which consist of small grassland and wetland units intended to preserve habitat for native
waterfowl, waterbirds, and other native migratory birds (USFWS, 2026k). Along with benefiting
migratory birds, WPAs also help sustain native plant communities. WPAs are acquired as public
lands or protected through easements within the USFWS National Wildlife Refuge System. WPAs
are primarily located within the prairie wetlands or potholes of the Dakotas, Minnesota, and
Montana, referred to as the Prairie Pothole Region, which holds 95 percent of USFWS WPAs
(USFWS, 2026k). A number of WPAs will be crossed by the Project (see table 3.1.1-4).

3.1.2   Impacts and Mitigation

3.1.2.1 Construction

Construction of the Project will require the use of a temporary construction right-of-way, and
operation of the pipelines will require retention of a permanent easement. WBI Energy proposes
to use a 125-foot-wide temporary construction right-of-way for 42-, 36-, or 30-inch-diameter
pipeline. The 20-inch-diameter pipeline will require a 100-foot-wide temporary construction right-
of-way. The temporary construction right-of-way will be 75 feet wide through wetland areas and
during construction of all other pipeline facilities. The permanent easement will be 50 feet wide.
Areas of additional temporary workspace (ATWS) will be required at wetland and waterbody
crossings; road and railroad crossings; points of inflection along the route; areas where special
construction methods will be implemented (e.g., the HDD or bore crossing methods); and areas
where additional space is needed for storage of stripped topsoil. Resource Reports 1 and 8
provide more information regarding land that will be affected by the construction and operation of
the pipelines.

Impacts on USFWS easements will be minimal, due to requirements for avoidance via trenchless
crossing methods (B. Gillis., USFWS, pers. comm. April 23, 2025). Some upland areas may be
crossed via open-cut methods, and impacts on specific vegetation types would be as discussed
below. WBI Energy is currently consulting with the USFWS to avoid impacts on easements in the
agency’s jurisdiction.

WBI Energy is coordinating with the BLM and USFS regarding the pipeline crossings across these
federal lands and will continue to coordinate with applicable agencies to minimize impacts
associated with any pipeline easements. Where possible, trenchless crossing methods will be
employed to avoid impacts to potential protective habitat under BLM or USFWS jurisdiction.

Clearing and grading of the construction right-of-way and temporary workspaces, along with
vehicle movement, will have temporary to long-term impacts on vegetation through vegetation
removal, crushing, compaction, and soil disturbance. Accidental spills of oil and fuel could
contaminate soils and harm vegetation. Table 3.1.1-1 provides vegetation (land cover) types
affected by construction activities in the construction right-of-way, ATWS, construction yards and
staging areas; aboveground facilities; and new and upgraded temporary and permanent access
roads.

Construction will primarily affect cropland and grassland, with smaller amounts of shrubland,
forest, wetland, and hay or pasture. WBI Energy has routed the proposed pipelines to avoid
native grasslands to the extent practicable. The use of HDD and bore construction methods will
minimize and/or avoid impacts on wetlands, native grassland, and other vegetation types. HDD
will be used in numerous riparian woodlands, which generally avoids the need for tree removal
except to clear vegetation for line-of-sight and guide-wire placement during the HDD process. As
described in Resource Report 7, topsoil will be segregated during grading and excavation and
replaced following construction to facilitate revegetation. During construction, bare soil will be

stabilized in accordance with conditions of the Project stormwater permit and FERC’s Upland
Erosion Control, Revegetation, and Maintenance Plan (Plan) and Wetland and Waterbody
Construction and Mitigation Procedures (Procedures). WBI Energy will revegetate disturbed non-
agricultural upland areas within the construction right-of-way and temporary workspaces following
construction in accordance with the FERC Plan and Procedures using seed mixes recommended
by the NRCS, landowners, or other appropriate agencies. Surfaces will be returned to
preconstruction grades to the extent feasible, and soils in cultivated fields will be decompacted
as needed in accordance with landowner agreements. Erosion and sediment control measures
will be implemented throughout construction in accordance with the stormwater permit(s) and
FERC Plan and Procedures, and the risk of adverse effects from spills of oil and fuel will be
minimized through implementation of the Project Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure
Plan (SPCC Plan). Other minimization measures to reduce impacts on wetland and upland soils
are discussed in Resource Reports 2 and 7.

Impacts on vegetation will range from temporary to long-term following construction. Herbaceous
(non-cultivated) vegetation is expected to re-establish within 3 to 5 years after seeding.
Shrublands would likely take 5 to 10 years to re-establish, and trees 10 to 20 years or longer.
Challenges to revegetation include wind and water erosion and poor-quality soil, particularly in
the Badlands with its steep slopes and high erosion rates, as well as in areas with droughty soil
(see Resource Report 7). Soil compaction may reduce germination and plant establishment in
the short term. In addition, construction equipment traveling from weed-infested areas onto
exposed soils in construction workspaces, along with other mechanisms of dispersal, could result
in the spread and establishment of invasive plants and noxious weeds.

WBI Energy will implement erosion and sediment control measures appropriate to the local
topography and will plant cover crops or otherwise stabilize soils to reduce wind and water erosion
(see Resource Reports 6 and 7). The measures described in the Project Noxious Weeds
Management Plan (appendix 1F, Resource Report 1) will help prevent and control the introduction
or spread of invasive and noxious weeds during and following construction of the Project.
Following construction, the Project area will be monitored in accordance with the FERC Plan and
Procedures, and noxious weed infestations within the Project area will be treated. WBI Energy
will prevent the spread of vegetative invasive ANS by crossing ANS-infested waterbodies using
HDD/bore methods in accordance with the Project Aquatic Nuisance Species Prevention Plan,
included in appendix 1F of Resource Report 1.

3.1.2.2 Operation

Approximately 2,440.1 acres will be retained for operation of the Project, including 2,275.0 acres
for the permanent 50-foot-wide right-of-way (table 3.1.1-1). Vegetation will be permanently
removed in the 140.8 acres covered by aboveground facilities and 23.0 acres by new and
expanded permanent access roads. The majority of the permanent right-of-way will be allowed
to return to preexisting conditions, including natural grassland, shrubland, and wetland vegetation
as well as cultivated crops and hayfields or pasture. In non-cultivated uplands, the entire 50-foot-
wide permanent easement will be maintained in an herbaceous state. The FERC Plan and
Procedures do not allow routine vegetation maintenance clearing more frequently than every
3 years, with the exception of a 15-foot-wide corridor centered over the pipelines, which can be
maintained annually in an herbaceous state to facilitate periodic corrosion and leak surveys. In
wetlands, the FERC Procedures allow for a 10-foot-wide corridor centered over the pipelines to
be permanently maintained in an herbaceous state, and trees greater than 15 feet in height within
15 feet of the pipelines may be cut and removed from the right-of-way. WBI Energy anticipates

3.2       WILDLIFE RESOURCES

This section provides an analysis of general wildlife that could be affected by the Project, along
with wildlife conservation areas. Wildlife and wildlife habitat that may occur in the Project area
were determined based on a desktop review of publicly available resources, including available
literature and agency websites (e.g., the NDGFD), a review of aerial photographs, and field
surveys. Endangered and threatened species are discussed in section 3.5.

3.2.1     Existing Wildlife Resources

3.2.1.1 General Wildlife

This section provides an analysis of mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and insects common to the
ecoregions that will be crossed by the Project. Birds are addressed in section 3.3, and fish and
other aquatic and semi-aquatic species are discussed in section 3.4.

As noted in section 3.1, the Project occurs in five of the ecosystems identified in the North Dakota
SWAP (NDGFD, 2025a). Within these ecosystems, the Project will cross six general NLCD land
cover classes providing distinct wildlife habitats (USGS, 2016). The vegetation classes and their
associated habitats include:

      •   agricultural land (cultivated crops);
      •   open land or grasslands (hayfields, pasture, short- and mixed-grass prairie, shrubland);
      •   forest (deciduous, evergreen, and mixed forests);
      •   developed land (low, high, and medium intensity development);
      •   open water; and
      •   wetlands (forested and non-forested).

The majority of the Project area occurs in agricultural land and grassland habitat. Woodland
habitat primarily occurs in riparian areas at perennial waterbody crossings and in the western
portion of the Project in the Badlands. Characteristic wildlife species of these and other habitats
present in the Project area that are not classified as species of conservation concern are
discussed below. Species currently listed as threatened, endangered, or special concern species
are discussed in section 3.5 of this report.

Big game species in North Dakota include bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis), white-tailed deer
(Odocoileus virginianus), mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus), elk (Cervus elaphus), moose (Alces
alces), and pronghorn (Antilocapra americana) (NDGFD, 2025g).

The NDGFD further categorizes game species as ungulates, furbearers, other mammals,
waterfowl, and other game birds (NDGFD, 2025h).

Agricultural Land

As discussed in section 3.1.1, 48.2 percent of the Project area consists of land converted to
agricultural use, including cropland, hayfields, and pasture. Despite the conversion of natural
habitats to introduced vegetation in these areas, many game and non-game wildlife species
inhabit the grassy and wooded edges of farmland and adjacent riparian and wetland habitat.
Agricultural areas bordered by shrubland or hedgerows and pastures tend to have greater species
diversity due to the availability of a wider variety of foraging, nesting, roosting, and cover habitats.

In general, cropland and hayfields provide poor quality wildlife habitat in the Project area given
the lack of plant diversity and high level of disturbance. While these areas tend to support
relatively low wildlife diversity, croplands may provide a food source for opportunistic species such
as the coyote (Canis latrans), white-tailed and mule deer, and raccoon (Procyon lotor). They also
provide habitat for reptiles like the plains spadefoot toad (Spea bombifrons) and short-horned
lizard (Phrynosoma douglassi) (NDGFD, 2025a; 2025d). In addition, land modified by agriculture
but left fallow can serve as surrogate habitat for bird species typically found in grasslands
(NRCS, 1999).

Grasslands and Shrublands

As discussed in section 3.1.1, 34.8 percent of the Project area consists of grassland and
shrubland. These habitats have higher plant diversity and a lower level of disturbance than
agricultural lands, providing wildlife with a greater variety of foraging, nesting, roosting, and cover
habitats. Game animals that inhabit grasslands in the Project area include mule deer, white-tailed
deer, elk, and pronghorn. Other typical wildlife species include coyote, badger (Taxidea taxus),
and several types of voles (e.g., prairie vole [Microtus spp.]) and squirrels (e.g., red squirrel
[Tamiasciurus hudsonicus]). In addition, several reptiles and amphibians inhabit grasslands, such
as the plains spadefoot toad and short-horned lizard. Many of these species are prey animals for
raptors. Grasslands and shrublands also provide breeding and migratory stopover habitat for a
large number of bird species (see section 3.3).

As noted in section 3.1.1.1, much of the grassland and shrubland in the Project area consists of
disturbed rangeland and previously farmed areas, although there are areas that retain the habitat
characteristics of native grassland. There are a number of federally listed and State Species of
Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) species dependent on native grassland.

Forest

As discussed in section 3.1.1, approximately 1 percent of the Project area is forest, most of which
is deciduous with a small amount of mixed forest. In the Project area, forests primarily occur as
narrow riparian woodlands, along with some upland forest in the badlands (NDGFD, 2025d).
Trees provide food, cover, and reproductive habitat for a variety of bird and mammal species.
Secondary canopy shrubs and saplings, brush piles, and fallen logs provide cover for a number
of small- to medium-sized mammals. Common mammal species that may be found in forests in
the Project area include the fisher (Pekania pennanti), flying squirrel (Glaucomys sabrinus), and
Virginia opossum (Didelphis virginiana) (NDGFD, 2025a; 2025d).

Developed Land

Developed land, which includes roads, railroads, and utility corridors, comprises about 6.3 percent
of the Project Area (see table 3.1.1-1). These areas generally provide poor habitat for wildlife due

to the lack of natural vegetation and residential, business, and industrial infrastructure. Typical
wildlife species that may be found in developed land within the Project area include opportunistic
mammal species acclimated to human disturbance, such as the coyote, fox squirrel (Sciurus
niger), raccoon, and weasel species (Neogale frenata, Mustela erminea, and Mustela nivalis)
(NDGFD, 2025a; 2025d).

Open Water

Aquatic habitat is limited in North Dakota given the relatively low amount of precipitation in the
state. Open water makes up less than 1 percent of the Project area and is largely seasonal,
consisting primarily of ephemeral and intermittent waterbodies, with a small number of perennial
streams, rivers, and lakes (see section 3.1.1 and Resource Report 2). In addition to fish and other
aquatic organisms, a number of mammals, reptiles, and amphibians depend on aquatic habitat.
Some mammal species such as the beaver (Castor canadensis) and muskrat (Ondatra
zibethicus) depend on aquatic habitat for food, reproduction, and shelter. Open water provides
an essential drinking water source for most wildlife (NDGFD 2025a; 2025d).

Wetlands

Wetland habitat primarily occurs in the eastern portion of the Project in the Prairie Pothole Region
(Missouri Couteau, Drift Prairie, and Red River Valley Ecoregions) and makes up approximately
1.8 percent of the Project area. It consists primarily of PEM, with less than 1 percent consisting
of PSS/PFO wetlands. A variety of amphibian species, such as the Canadian toad (Anaxyrus
hemiophrys), rely on wetlands for breeding habitat. Wetlands also provide year-round habitat for
mammals such as muskrats and support large populations of waterfowl and waterbirds (see
section 3.3) (NDGFD 2025a; 2025d).

3.2.1.2 Big Game

Big game species, such as bighorn sheep, white-tailed or mule deer, elk, moose, and pronghorn,
may be impacted by construction of the Project. The Project intersects the bighorn sheep range,
mule deer primary and secondary range, elk range, and pronghorn secondary range at the start
of the proposed mainline route to the west. It intersects the moose primary range near the end
of the proposed mainline route to the east (NDGFD, 2025g).

Other game species include upland game species like squirrels, and furbearers like the badger ,
beaver, bobcat (Lynx rufus), coyote, fisher , red fox (Vulpes vulpes), mink (Mustela vison),
mountain lion (Puma concolor), muskrat, raccoon, river otter (Lontra canadensis), and weasels
(NDGFD, 2025a; 2025h). For furbearers, prime fur periods generally begin in November and can
extend as late as March for some species (NDGFD, 2025i).

3.2.1.3 Conservation Areas

There are no National Wild and Scenic Rivers or state-designated high quality or outstanding
natural resource waters crossed by the Project (National Wild and Scenic Rivers System, 2026).

Conservation Areas discussed in Section 3.1.1.3 for vegetation also provide valuable wildlife
habitat, including USDA and USFWS conservation easements on private lands, USFWS WPAs
on private and public lands, BLM lands, and the LMNG. NDGFD WMAs have regulations for
motor vehicle use, watercraft use, and removal and destruction of property; however, no WMAs
are crossed by the Project (NDGFD, 2025f).

3.2.2   Impacts and Mitigation

3.2.2.1 Construction

As discussed in section 3.1.2.1, the temporary construction right-of-way will be up to 125 feet
wide depending on the pipeline diameter. Construction activities within the right-of-way will
temporarily reduce feeding, nesting, and cover options for common wildlife and big game in the
immediate Project area. Mobile species may be temporarily disturbed or displaced from portions
of their habitats, and injury or mortality of individuals of less mobile species, such as some small
mammals, reptiles or amphibians, and young wildlife, may occur. Construction noise and
increased human activity could result in wildlife displacement and avoidance of work areas. Since
this is a linear project, construction impacts on wildlife along the proposed pipeline routes and in
other work areas will generally be of short duration at any given location. Given the temporary
impacts, disruptions to big game migration and breeding seasons would not be expected to occur.
Blasting is not expected to be needed, but in the event that it becomes necessary, WBI Energy’s
Blasting Plan will be implemented (see Resource Report 1 appendix 1F).

Protected wildlife habitats may be affected by the Project. WBI Energy was able to avoid USFWS
grassland easements and adjust portions of the route to avoid USFWS wetland easements. While
a number of wetland easements are still crossed by the proposed Project within the USFWS
Audubon, Long Lake, Chase, and Valley City Wetland Management Districts, WBI Energy will
avoid or minimize potential impacts to protected wetlands within the easements by implementing
trenchless crossing methods (HDD or bore methods described in section 1.3.2.1 of Resource
Report 1) to the greatest extent practicable, minimizing disturbance to wetland- or waterbody-
reliant species.

The majority of the Project occurs in agricultural land and grassland habitat. As noted, most
impacts will be to wildlife using cultivated cropland, grasslands, and shrublands. WBI Energy
avoided forest habitat and native grasslands to the greatest extent possible during Project design,
including through the use of HDD in certain riparian woodlands, which generally does not result
in substantial tree removal (see section 3.1.1).

The loss of cropland and hayfield habitats will be temporary because crops would be allowed to
be replanted the year after construction is completed. The loss of pasture, grassland, shrubland,
and PEM wetland habitat will be relatively short term since WBI Energy will reseed and restore
disturbed areas following construction (see section 3.1.2). Given the abundant adjacent habitat
available on either side of the right-of-way and the short-term nature of impacts, no changes to
wildlife populations dependent on cropland, pasture, grassland, shrubland, and wetland habitats
are anticipated. Long-term impacts are associated with removal of forest habitat (see section
3.1.2.2). Following construction, trees in the temporary construction right-of-way will be allowed

Operational activities will be limited to periodically conducting vegetation maintenance within the

3.3     AVIAN RESOURCES

3.3.1   Existing Avian Resources

3.3.1.1 Non-Migratory Birds

Common non-migratory grassland species of birds include several species of upland gamebirds
(e.g., greater sage-grouse [Centrocercus urophasianus], greater prairie-chicken [Tympanuchus
cupido], sharp-tailed grouse [Tympanuchus phasianellus], and ring-necked pheasant [Phasianus
colchicus]) and upland birds of prey (e.g., prairie falcon [Falco mexicanus], short-eared owl [Asio
flammeus] and golden eagle [Aquila chrysaetos]). Nearly all grassland songbirds are migratory
(NDGFD, 2025c). Several non-migratory grassland bird species and upland birds of prey are
classified as SGCN, including the greater sage grouse, greater prairie-chicken, sharp-tailed
grouse, prairie falcon, short-eared owl, and golden eagle (NDGFD, 2025a).

3.3.1.2 Migratory Birds

The Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) is a strict liability statute that imposes penalties for
noncompliance. The act makes it “unlawful at any time, by any means or in any manner” to,
among other things, pursue, hunt, take, capture, kill, or attempt to take, capture, or kill, any
migratory bird or any part, nest, or eggs of such a bird (16 U.S.C. § 703 et seq.). Non-native
birds are not covered by the MBTA. Section 3 of the 2001 Executive Order 13186 directs federal
agencies to promote migratory bird population conservation, which includes an analysis of the
effects of actions on migratory birds, emphasizing species of conservation concern.

The question of whether incidental take is prohibited by the MBTA remains uncertain due to recent
conflicting presidential, USFWS, and federal court determinations (2001 Executive Order 13186;
2020 Natural Resources Defense Council v. U.S. Department of the Interior; 2021 USFWS
Director’s Order 225; 2025 USFWS memorandum M-37085). WBI Energy will coordinate with
the USFWS to minimize the risk of incidental take of migratory birds.

A variety of migratory bird species may occur seasonally along the proposed pipeline routes. The
Project is within the Central Flyway for waterfowl (USFWS, 2021b; 2025b). Many species of
migratory birds such as ducks, geese, doves, and pigeons, as well as sandhill cranes (Antigone
canadensis) and tundra swans (Cygnus columbianus), use the flyway during spring and fall
migration between the Gulf of Mexico and central Canada (USFWS, 2025b). Many migratory
populations use open land and wetland areas as stopover habitat.

The Prairie Pothole region is particularly important for providing breeding and migration stopover
habitat for waterbirds, shorebirds, and waterfowl. The region typically sustains up to 10 million

3.3.1.3 Bald and Golden Eagles

The Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act (BGEPA) (16 U.S. Code 688) provides additional
protection to bald and golden eagles. The BGEPA prohibits the take, possession, sale, barter,
offer to sell, purchase, transport, export, or import of any bald or golden eagle, alive or dead—


                                                               3-21
                                                                     Bakken East Pipeline Project
                                                Resource Report 3 – Fish, Wildlife, and Vegetation

including any part, nest, or egg, unless allowed by permit. “Take” under this act is defined as “to
pursue, shoot, shoot at, poison, wound, kill, capture, trap, collect, or molest or disturb.” Disturb
is defined as “to agitate or bother a bald or golden eagle to a degree that causes, or is likely to
cause, based on the best scientific information available, (1) injury to an eagle, (2) a decrease in
its productivity, by substantially interfering with normal breeding, feeding, or sheltering behavior,
or (3) nest abandonment, by substantially interfering with normal breeding, feeding, or sheltering
behavior.”
The USFWS may issue permits for activities impacting nesting bald eagles (50 CFR Parts 13 and
22). A nest take permit is required for any activity that removes, relocates, destroys, or obstructs
an eagle nest, even if the nest is not in use. A general permit for bald eagle disturbance is typically
recommended for construction activities within 660 feet of an active bald eagle nest during and
outside of the breeding season (USFWS, 2026a). Extremely loud activities, such as blasting,
may expand the buffer for permit coverage. Current USFWS recommendations for protecting
breeding golden eagles from human disturbance call for 0.5-mile avoidance buffers around active
nests; however, NDGFD guidance indicates that buffers are determined based on the variables
of the project location, and the USFWS notes that impacts could occur further than 0.5 mile
depending on the circumstances (NDGFD, 2009; USFWS, 2010; 2017; 2024b). Unlike bald
eagles (which have established guidelines), golden eagle buffer zones are highly variable; safe
buffer distances depend on the scope of work, local topography, noise levels, and visibility from
the nest.
Bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) inhabit riparian areas close to water, and in tall trees.
Golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) inhabit areas where open or semi-open features are present,
such as prairies or sparse woodland. Bald eagles are most likely to occur in riparian areas for
nesting and breeding, while golden eagles prefer cliffs and rock ledges for nesting (NatureServe,
2026). Golden eagles are also listed in the NDGFD SWAP as a SGCN for the Badlands Ecoregion
and for the Little Missouri River Focus Area (NDGFD, 2025a).
WBI Energy reviewed golden eagle nesting habitat data available from the NDGFD (NDGFD,
2022), which shows suitable nesting habitat for golden eagles crossed or in the vicinity of the
Project in the Badlands, generally between mileposts 6 and 28. The NDGFD data showed no
known golden eagle nests within 1.0 mile of the Project and no known bald eagle nests within
660 feet of the Project.
3.3.2   Impacts and Mitigation

3.3.2.1 Construction

Non-Migratory and Migratory Birds
Potential construction impacts on non-migratory and migratory birds include temporary habitat
fragmentation, temporary habitat loss, construction disturbance, and injury or mortality. Birds
would be most susceptible to harm from disturbance and injury or mortality during the breeding
season. Construction disturbance and loud noise could cause adults to abandon their nests
permanently or for extended periods of time, while eggs and young birds incapable of flight would
be unable to move out of the way of construction equipment and vehicles.
The majority of habitat affected by the Project will be to grassland habitat. Ground-nesting birds,
such as the ring-necked pheasant, the Canada goose (Branta canadensis), Hungarian partridge
(Perdix perdix), and mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) are therefore most likely to be affected by the
Project since they are common in grassland habitat or cropland. Grasslands also provide habitat
to raptors like the red-tailed hawk (Buteo jamaicensis), northern harrier, and prairie falcon. Mixed-

grass prairie is important breeding habitat for sharp-tailed grouse. Several neotropical migratory
songbirds prefer to nest in open herbaceous vegetation including the western meadowlark,
chestnut-collared longspur, grasshopper sparrow, and lark bunting . The low-lying vegetation in
grasslands provides necessary habitat structure for protection from predators and brood-rearing
activities. Grasslands provide a variety of forage food sources for migrating birds such as insects
and other invertebrates, fruits, and native grass seeds.
Forested areas provide habitat for birds such as the hooded merganser (Lophodytes cucullatus).
The American kestrel (Falco sparverius), brown thrasher (Toxostoma rufum), Harris’s sparrow
(Zonotrichia querula), and loggerhead shrike (Lanius ludovicianus) are the only bird species with
a range including developed lands (NDGFD, 2025d).
Impacts on habitat include the potential temporary disturbance of soils and vegetation during
construction. Direct impacts on species include the potential for mortality or injury during
construction from destruction of ground nests or vehicle collisions.
To minimize impacts in areas where clearing cannot occur outside of the peak migratory bird
nesting season, WBI Energy will conduct surveys for nesting birds within 7 days prior to clearing
of the right-of-way. If nests are identified during surveys, WBI Energy will set up avoidance buffers
around the nest to minimize disturbance. If needed, a biological monitor will oversee construction
around the nest to determine whether the level of disturbance has been adequately minimized to
reduce the risk that the nest could fail. Construction activities in these areas could resume once
the chicks have fledged or the nest is no longer active. In areas where clearing occurs prior to
migratory bird nesting but construction does not occur right after clearing, the construction area
will be maintained (as needed) to avoid the regrowth of potential nesting habitat.
After construction is complete, WBI Energy will restore the right-of-way to preconstruction
condition in accordance with the FERC Plan and Procedures. Cropland will be restored to active
agricultural production, and other areas will be revegetated using methods and seed mixes
appropriate to existing land uses and cover types. WBI Energy anticipates that the Project area
will recover to pre-disturbance conditions over time. Consequently, the Project will not
permanently alter the character of available habitats for migratory birds.
Eagles
Prior to the start of construction, WBI Energy will complete incidental raptor nest ground surveys
within 1 mile of the Project area if suitable nesting habitat, landscape features, and the likelihood
of the species are present; additionally, WBI Energy will review available NDGFD nesting habitat
data. If an active bald eagle nest is identified within 660 feet of the Project area, WBI Energy will
implement the measures described in the USFWS’s 2007 National Bald Eagle Management
Guidelines (USFWS, 2007) and USFWS avoidance recommendations to avoid disturbance take.
If an active golden eagle nest is identified within 1.0 mile of the Project area, WBI Energy will
coordinate with the USFWS to determine if a buffer greater than 0.5 mile should be evaluated and
if take could occur. If disturbance take cannot be avoided for either bald or golden eagles, WBI
Energy will coordinate with the USFWS to obtain an incidental disturbance permit. Based on
implementation of these measures and the lack of documented nests within the avoidance
buffers, the Project is not expected to result in the take of bald or golden eagles.

3.4     FISHERIES AND OTHER AQUATIC RESOURCES
This section describes potential impacts on fisheries and other aquatic resources (aquatic
resources) that occur within the Project area, including general aquatic resources and commercial
and recreational fisheries. Information on aquatic habitat and organisms within the Project area
was obtained from available literature, resources from the NDGFD, and other publicly available
information.
Fisheries of special concern are discussed in section 3.5 and include aquatic species identified
by the NDGFD as SGCN, protected under the federal ESA, or protected on federal lands in
accordance with federal land management plans.
3.4.1   Existing Aquatic Resources

3.4.1.1 General Fisheries and Aquatic Resources

Aquatic habitat is limited in the Project area. North Dakota has a moderately dry continental
climate, with cold, dry winters and annual precipitation ranging from 13 to 20 inches a year
(NDGFD, 2025y). The state supports freshwater aquatic habitat in intermittent and perennial
streams, wetlands, ponds, and lakes with bottom sediments consisting of sand, gravel, and/or silt.
The vast majority (92 percent) of streams in North Dakota are ephemeral or intermittent streams
that are dry for most of the year (EPA, 2013). There is no essential fish habitat regulated under
the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act in North Dakota. None of the
waterbodies in the Project area are classified as marine or estuarine waters, and none has the
potential to contain anadromous or catadromous species.
The Project lies within four Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC)-4 subregions associated with the Missouri
and Little Missouri Rivers (the Missouri/Little Missouri and Missouri-Oahe HUC-4 subregions), the
James River (James HUC-4 subregion), and the Red River (Red HUC-4 subregion). Within the
subregions of these larger rivers, the Project will cross 42 HUC-10 watersheds involving
196 waterbody crossings, including 157 ephemeral/intermittent stream crossings, 14 perennial
stream crossings (including connector and artificial paths where engineering has altered the
waterbody route or bed and banks), 5 canal/ditch crossings, and 20 lake or pond crossings (see
section 2.2.1 of Resource Report 2). Some waterbodies have multiple crossings.

The quality of aquatic habitat crossed by the Project is generally low. Section 2.2.2 of Resource
Report 2 describes the water quality classification systems (Class I, IA, II, and III) in North Dakota,
with Class I/IA having the highest water quality in regard to the propagation and/or protection of
resident fish species and other aquatic biota, and Classes II and III having limited value as aquatic
habitat. Class II and III waterbodies are typically intermittent streams, with Class III having the
lowest average flows with prolonged periods of no flow (North Dakota Department of
Environmental Quality [NDDEQ], 2018). The water quality of lakes and reservoirs (lakes) has a
similar ranking system in North Dakota based on the value of aquatic habitat:

   •   Class 1 lakes support cold water fish species and associated aquatic biota (based partly
       on size and depth);

   •   Class 2 lakes support cool water fish species and associated aquatic biota;

   •   Class 3 lakes support warm water fish species and associated aquatic biota;

   •   Class 4 lakes can support fish only on a short-term or seasonal bases (i.e., from stocking);
       and

   •   Class 5 lakes are unable to support fish (NDDEQ, 2018).

As detailed in table 2B-1 of Resource Report 2, the majority of waterbodies crossed by the Project
have limited value as aquatic habitat, with 159 crossings of Class III streams, 13 crossings of
Class II streams, and 7 crossings of Class I/IA streams. None of the waterbodies affected by the
Project are lakes or reservoirs that are classified or managed based on their ability to sustain
fishery resources.
While wetlands are not an important source of habitat for fisheries in North Dakota, they do
provide important habitat for aquatic invertebrates. The Project will cross 408 wetlands, a majority
of which are palustrine emergent wetlands (PEM). However, the Project crosses lesser amounts
of palustrine forested (shrub) wetlands (Pf) and palustrine forested wetlands (PFO) (see
section 2.3 of Resource Report 2 for more information).
Descriptions of the respective assemblage of aquatic species associated with the various types
of aquatic habitat crossed by the Project are described in the following sections.
Ephemeral and Intermittent Streams
Ephemeral and intermittent waterbodies may provide low-quality, temporary nursery habitat for
warm-water forage fish and some recreational species. Common species found in this habitat
include fish such as the sand shiner (Miniellus stramineus), creek chub (Semotilus
atromaculatus), and flathead chub (Platygobio gracilis); reptiles such as the snapping turtle
(Chelydra serpentina); and invertebrates like the pink heelsplitter (Potamilus alatus) and fragile
papershell (Leptodea fragilis) (NDGFD, 2025d; 2025k).
Perennial Streams, Rivers, and Lakes
The majority of perennial streams, rivers, and lakes in North Dakota support warmwater fish
species and associated aquatic biota, with the exception of certain lakes and portions of the
Missouri River system that support coldwater species (NDGFD, 2025a; 2025d; 2025l).
Representative warmwater species in North Dakota found in perennial streams and rivers include
walleye (Stizostedion vitreum), northern pike (Esox lucius), largemouth bass (Micropterus
nigricans), and smallmouth bass (Micropterus dolomieu). Representative coldwater fish species

include lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush) and chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha) (All
About Fishing, 2026).
Freshwater habitat in North Dakota is also home to amphibians (such as the plains spadefoot
[Spea bombifrons]), reptiles (like snapping turtle and the spiny softshell turtle [Apalone spinifera]),
semi-aquatic mammals (like muskrat [Ondatra zibethicus]), and benthic macroinvertebrates
(BMIs), which are an essential part of the aquatic food chain (NDGFD, 2025a; 2025d). BMI
species in North Dakota include several species of mussel (such as the black sandshell [Ligumia
recta] and Wabash pigtoe [Fusconaia flava]), annelids (worms and leeches), and insects, which
provide an important food source for birds, bats, and other organisms (NDGFD, 2025a). Common
insects dependent on aquatic habitat in their larval stages include mayflies [Ephemeroptera],
stoneflies [Plecoptera], and flies [Diptera]) (NDGFD, 2012; 2025a). Perennial streams and rivers
and their shorelines also provide important stopover, foraging, and nesting habitat for waterbirds
and waterfowl, as discussed in section 3.2.1.1.
3.4.1.2 Recreational and Commercial Fisheries

North Dakota does not have a large commercial fishing industry. Fisheries in North Dakota are
managed primarily for recreational fishing and conservation. Important recreational fisheries
include numerous species, such as those listed above for perennial streams, rivers, lakes, and
ponds, along with other warm- and coldwater species (NDGFD, 2025m). While these species
may occur in perennial streams and lakes in the Project area, most of the waterbodies crossed
by the Project are not identified as recreational fishing locations. The NDGFD lists lakes and
rivers that support recreational fishing in the state. Of the waterbodies crossed by the Project,
the Missouri, Little Missouri, Knife, and Sheyenne Rivers, as well as the Jamestown Reservoir
and Eckelson Lake North, are identified as supporting recreational fishing (NDGFD, 2025m;
2025n).
There are two national fish hatcheries in North Dakota run by the USFWS and supported by the
NDGFD that serve as an important resource for stocking recreational fish as well as for fish
conservation. One of these, the Valley City National Fish Hatchery, is located along the Sheyenne
River approximately 0.25 mile from the Project corridor, 7 miles downstream of the proposed
Sheyenne River HDD crossing, and 1 mile downstream from the proposed open-cut crossing of
an unnamed perennial tributary to the Sheyenne River (USFWS, 2026i).
3.4.1.3 Invasive Species

Invasive aquatic species are regulated by the state under North Dakota Administrative Code
Chapter 30-03-06, which requires that all construction equipment used for in-water work must be
free of prohibited or regulated ANS, as identified in the state's ANS list. ANS that could occur in
waterbodies crossed by the Project based on their known distributions include common carp
(Cyprinus carpio) and zebra mussels (Dreissena polymorpha). Common carp are most likely to
be found in lakes and the lower portions of rivers, while zebra mussels can occur in most streams
and lakes (NDGFD, 2025e; 2025o; 2025p).
Of the waterbodies crossed by the Project, the Sheyenne River is documented to be infested with
zebra mussels. Common carp populations have confirmed presence in the Little Missouri,
Missouri, Sheyenne, and Knife Rivers that are crossed by the Project (NDGFD, 2025e; 2025o).

3.4.2   Impacts and Mitigation

3.4.2.1 Construction

Project construction has the potential to affect aquatic organisms and their habitats due to pipeline
and access road waterbody crossings, HDD/bore inadvertent returns, water withdrawals from
surface waters, and stormwater runoff or spills into aquatic habitat from upland construction areas,
as discussed in the following sections.
The pipeline will be installed across aquatic habitat through three primary methods: HDD, bore,
and open-cut (see section 1.3.2.1 of Resource Report 1), with the majority of waterbodies planned
to be crossed via the open-cut method. If any waterbodies along the pipeline routes cannot be
crossed by these methods, WBI Energy may implement the flume or dam-and-pump dry-ditch
crossing methods (see section 2.2.8.6, Resource Report 2). The exact crossing method may be
adjusted based on site-specific flow conditions at the time of construction. Table 2B-1 in appendix
2B of Resource Report 2 lists the state water quality classifications for waterbodies crossed by
the Project and the proposed crossing methods. The Project will cross 196 waterbodies, including
157 ephemeral/intermittent streams, 14 perennial streams, 5 canal/ditch crossings, and 20 lake
or pond crossings. Because most waterbodies are ephemeral or intermittent and are fed primarily
by snowmelt and spring rains, many will likely be dry by early to mid-summer.
WBI Energy will use trenchless crossing methods (HDD/bore) to avoid impacts on aquatic
habitats. HDD/bore entry and exit points will be placed in upland areas, and the pipe will be
installed below the waterbody. These methods will be used at larger perennial waterbodies and
303(d) streams. The HDD/bore crossing method could cause inadvertent returns of drilling fluids
to the waterbody. Drilling fluid will be composed of water mixed with in-situ material or bentonite,
not listed as a hazardous substance by the EPA; drilling fluid additives will be limited to non-
petrochemical based, non-hazardous additives currently certified to the American National
Standards Institute/National Sanitation Foundation International Standard 60. WBI Energy will
implement its Horizontal Directional Drill/Bore Drilling Fluid Monitoring and Operations Plan (HDD
Plan), provided in appendix 1F of Resource Report 1, which includes measures to prevent, detect,
and respond to inadvertent returns, such as containment and cleanup procedures, to minimize
effects on aquatic resources.
Open-cut and dry-ditch (e.g., flume or dam-and-pump) crossing methods will involve excavation
of a trench directly through the waterbody. Impacts on aquatic organisms could include temporary
modifications to aquatic habitat (e.g., stream bank excavation, in-stream trenching, dewatering,
and backfilling), increased turbidity, decreased dissolved oxygen concentrations, and disruption
of natural flow. These potential impacts are limited to the period of in-stream construction, and
conditions will return to normal shortly after restoration activities are complete. WBI Energy will
minimize effects on aquatic resources through completion of in-water construction within 24 hours
for open-cut minor waterbodies, and 48 hours for open-cut intermediate waterbodies. WBI Energy
will install erosion and sediment control devices to stabilize soils/capture sediment. Open-cut and
dry-ditch crossing methods will comply with the FERC Procedures, applicable permit
requirements, and local regulations.
Some existing access roads across waterbodies would require improvements, including culvert
replacement, that would involve in-water work. New access roads across waterbodies would
require temporary equipment bridges or culvert installation, both of which would involve in-water
work. Temporary equipment bridges (equipped with geotextile fabric underneath to capture
sediment) may be installed across waterbodies to reduce turbidity/sedimentation resulting from
equipment and vehicular traffic. Impacts would be similar to those described for pipeline

3.4.2.2 Operation

Project operation will have only minor effects on aquatic resources because the pipeline is placed
underground. There may be short- to long-term increases in water temperature in isolated areas

approximately 2 to 10 years, respectively. Trees would not be allowed to grow within 15 feet of
the pipeline, which could result in a permanent increase in water temperatures through reduced
shading in woodland areas (Leinenbach et al., 2015). At HDD crossings, trees would largely be
left undisturbed, although some hand clearing of trees and vegetation may be required between
the entry and exit sites to provide line-of-sight and facilitate guide wire placement during drilling
operations; however, the vegetation would be allowed to regrow following construction. Pipeline

3.5.1.1 Northern Long-eared Bat

Species Background
The northern long-eared bat (Myotis septentrionalis) (NLEB) ranges across the eastern and north
central United States, and all Canadian provinces west to the southern Yukon Territory and
eastern British Columbia (78 Federal Register [FR] 61046). NLEBs are considered common in
only small portions of the western part of its range (i.e., Black Hills of South Dakota) and
uncommon or rare in the western extremes of the range (78 FR 61046). While uncommon, there
have been recent NLEB detected occurrences in the southwestern portion of North Dakota (DOE,
2026), the riparian areas along the Little Missouri and Missouri Rivers, and forests in the Turtle
Mountains (NDGFD, 2025r).
During the summer, NLEB roost underneath bark and in cavities or crevices of live and dead
trees, in culverts, or under bridges. Summer roosting habitat is typically restricted to mature,
intact woodlands at least 5 acres in size with both dead/decaying and live trees with cavities or
exfoliating bark (USFWS 2022a). However, NLEBs may also roost in open structures such as



                                                                3-30
                                                                     Bakken East Pipeline Project
                                                Resource Report 3 – Fish, Wildlife, and Vegetation

buildings, barns, utility poles, bridges, and culverts (USFWS, 2022a; 2024). Suitable culverts are
likely greater than 4.5 feet in diameter/height and 23 feet in length, the typical width of a two-lane
road (USFWS, 2024d). The NLEB forms maternity colonies during the breeding season from late
May to mid-July that generally consist of 30 to 60 individuals (Caceres and Barclay, 2000;
Whitaker and Mumford, 2009; USFWS, 2022a). Juveniles are able to fly approximately 21 days
after birth (Krochmal and Sparks, 2007).
In North Dakota, summer roosting and foraging habitat primarily occurs along wooded riparian
corridors. The NLEB is known to occur along the Little Missouri and Missouri Rivers in North
Dakota, including in McKenzie, Dunn, Mercer, Oliver, and Burleigh Counties (NDGFD, 2025r).
NLEBs spend winter months hibernating in crevices or cracks of caves and mines. Bat
hibernacula can also include talus slopes or rock crevices, though less is known about the roosts
in these features as they are less accessible to surveyors (Bachen et al., 2019). There are no
known hibernacula within North Dakota (USFWS, 2026g); however, there has been limited survey
effort in the state (78 FR 61046). Potential habitat could include abandoned or active mines, the
former of which are plentiful on the western side of North Dakota (North Dakota Public Service
Commission, 2026). As of 2024, there are four active coal mines in North Dakota (U.S. Energy
Information Administration, 2025). The four mines are located near the cities of Center, Zap,
Beulah, and Falkirk (Lignite Energy Council, 2026). The Badlands are crossed by the western
portion of the Project and may provide cliff and crevice habitat (NDGFD, 2025b). The estimated
NLEB hibernation season in North Dakota is from November 1 through April 14 (USFWS, 2026f).
Historically, the Midwest Recovery Planning Unit is thought to contain nine (1 percent) of the
known NLEB hibernacula sites and 3 percent of the known wintering NLEB populations (USFWS,
2022a).
The NLEB is a threatened species under the ESA. The species is highly susceptible to white-
nose syndrome, which is estimated to be the cause of a 97 to 100 percent population decline
across the majority of the species’ range, including the Midwest (Cheng et al., 2021; USFWS
2022b). Other sources of mortality for the NLEB include impacts on winter hibernation areas, loss
or degradation of woodland habitat, and wind farm operations (USFWS, 2022b; NDGFD, 2025r).

3.5.1.2 Piping Plover

Species Background
Piping plovers (Charadrius melodus) of the Northern Great Plains breed along barren sand and
gravel shores of prairie rivers and alkali wetlands (USFWS, 2003; 2026h). North Dakota is the
most important state within the Great Plains region for nesting piping plovers. In North Dakota,
the majority of piping plovers nest on prairie alkali lakes, while others select the free-flowing
stretch of the Missouri River. Piping plovers also use barren river sandbars typically along the
Missouri and Yellowstone Rivers (USFWS, 2026h). Piping plovers arrive in North Dakota in early
to mid-April and remain until the end of August. The NDGFD predicts approximately 300 to 400
breeding pairs reside along the Missouri River System (NDGFD, 2025s).
The piping plover is a threatened species under the ESA. The recent decline in the Northern
Great Plains piping plover population is attributed to the destruction of vegetated sandbars and
river islands for flood control and navigation, water level regulation policies that endanger nesting
habitat, direct disturbance by people, and poor breeding success, primarily because of an
increase in predator abundance (USFWS, 2026h).
Nineteen areas of critical habitat for the Northern Great Plains population of the piping plover
have been designated by the USFWS (67 FR 57638), totaling about 183,422 acres in Minnesota,
Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, and South Dakota. Within the Project area, the Missouri River
(North Dakota Critical Habitat Unit 11) is designated piping plover critical habitat. Adjacent to the
Project, North Dakota Critical Habitat Units 7 (Burleigh and Kidder Counties) and 8 (Stutsman
County) also feature designated piping plover critical habitat. The habitat features present in
these critical habit units that are essential to the conservation of the species include sparsely
vegetated sandbars and shorelines, and alkali lakes and wetlands with surrounding shoreline.
Impacts and Mitigation
Piping plovers arrive in the Project area in April for mating and nesting and migrate south in
August. Because construction of the Project is anticipated to occur year-round, the piping plover
breeding and nesting season will overlap with the Project construction timeline, and it is possible
that nesting birds will be present during construction. Activity occurring within 0.5 mile of an active
nest has the potential to adversely affect nesting piping plovers. Therefore, noise, visual, and
physical disturbances from Project activity may affect essential mating, nesting, and foraging
behaviors of piping plovers. Pipeline construction is currently planned to begin in early 2029.

3.5.1.3 Rufa Red Knot

Species Background
In North America, rufa red knots (Calidris canutus rufa) are commonly found in marine habitats
and coastal areas along sandy, gravel, or cobble beaches, tidal mudflats, salt marshes, shallow
coastal impoundments and lagoons, and peat banks (USFWS, 2014). Rufa red knots have been
documented along the Northern Plains during their spring migration (USFWS, 2014) and they
have been tracked along the central flyway with geolocators. The rufa red knot is considered a
rare migrant in North Dakota, but may pass through in mid-May and mid-September to October
during spring and fall migrations. The estimated migration population in North Dakota is less than
100 individuals (NDGFD, 2025t). Rufa red knots have been observed along shorelines of the
Missouri River, sewage lagoons, and large permanent freshwater wetlands but there are no
known, consistently used stopover sites in North Dakota (NDGFD, 2025t). There is a lack of
information on the specific noncoastal habitats used by rufa red knots (USFWS, 2014); however,
given their specialized molluscivore diet, it can be assumed they would use shallow wetlands,
lake margins, and riverine habitats within North Dakota for foraging and/or roosting areas.
The rufa red knot is a threatened species under the ESA. Rufa red knot populations have declined
due to degradation of wetland areas, reduced food availability, expanding oil and gas
development that overlaps migration ranges, and contamination to alkali lakes and the Missouri
River system (USFWS, 2014; NDGFD, 2025t).
Impacts and Mitigation
The rufa red knot is considered a rare migrant in North Dakota, but may pass through the state in
mid-May and mid-September to October during spring and fall migrations. Similar to the effects
on the piping plover, there may be migrant birds present during year-round construction. Noise,
visual, or physical disturbance from the Project may cause species dispersal to adjacent habitat.
WBI Energy will continue to assess the likelihood of presence and the potential for adverse effects
through development of a Biological Assessment, to be submitted with the final application. A
final impact determination and conservation measures will be identified through Section 7
consultation with the USFWS to ensure compliance with the ESA.
3.5.1.4 Whooping Crane

Species Background
The whooping crane (Grus americana) utilizes a variety of habitats along their migration route,
including croplands, freshwater wetlands with shallow areas, and submerged sandbars in wide,
unobstructed river channels isolated from human disturbance (Austin and Richert, 2005; Urbanek
and Lewis, 2020). The Aransas-Wood Buffalo population of the whooping crane migrates in the
spring and fall through the central portion of North Dakota. Spring migration occurs from late April
to mid-June, with most sightings occurring in the western two-thirds of the state. During migration,
